A_target.statement:
Let $M$ be a [[Definition:Closed Manifold|closed]] [[Definition:Oriented Manifold|oriented]] $n$-[[Definition:Topological Manifold|manifold]] and $F$ a [[Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)|field]].
Then:
:$\map {H_k} {M; F} \cong \map {H^{n - k} } {M; F}$

B_source.statement:
Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional [[Definition:Vector Space|vector spaces]] over $F$ with a [[Definition:Nondegenerate Bilinear Form|nondegenerate]] [[Definition:Bilinear Mapping|bilinear pairing]] $V \times W \to F$.
Then:
:$V \cong W^*$

substitutions.the nondegenerate pairing: the intersection pairing of complementary-dimensional cycles
substitutions.the second space of the pairing: homology in degree n minus k

derived.each space is identified with the dual o: homology in degree k is dual to homology in complementary degree

object_map.reformulation: Read the geometric intersection of complementary cycles as a nondegenerate pairing, which identifies each side with the other's dual.

validity_conditions: Cycles of complementary dimension meet in finitely many points, and orientation lets those intersections be counted with consistent signs, which makes the pairing well defined.
Closedness is required so there is no boundary into which cycles can escape, and orientability is required for the signs to be globally consistent.
The pairing is nondegenerate over a field; over the integers torsion obstructs the naive statement and the correct formulation involves a separate linking pairing.
proof_plan: Define the [[Definition:Intersection Pairing|intersection pairing]] $\map {H_k} M \times \map {H_{n - k} } M \to F$ by counting, with signs given by the orientation, the transverse intersection points of cycles of complementary dimension.

Homologous cycles have intersection counts differing by the boundary of a $1$-chain of intersection points, which is zero.
As $M$ is closed and oriented, the pairing is well-defined on homology classes.
With field coefficients, the pairing is [[Definition:Nondegenerate Bilinear Form|nondegenerate]], as follows from dual cell decompositions of $M$.

By the source result, $\map {H_k} M \cong \map {H_{n - k} } M^*$.
By the [[Universal Coefficient Theorem]] over a field, $\map {H_{n - k} } M^* \cong \map {H^{n - k} } M$.
This is [[Poincaré Duality]].
{{qed}}
